name: Colin Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and an experienced developer on greenhouse irrigation software for a tech company, with a bachelor’s degree. I use AI every day to draft sensor checks but still compare alerts with the plants in a real greenhouse. My wife Ana runs a nursery; we have a mortgage and two school-age children, and I like solving a dry-bed warning before a grower loses the crop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a little AI can write sensor checks, but someone still needs to notice when the greenhouse soil is dry. I use AI daily for code drafts and compare each alert with the reading from a real bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a bachelor’s degree, ordinary pay for an experienced developer, and about five months of basic bills saved. My wife Ana runs a plant nursery; with two school-age children and a mortgage, her spring sales matter but my wage is steady for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing the irrigation alerts and visit Ana’s nursery once a month to compare the app with her paper watering chart. We would keep saving 140 monthly if my pay and her sales hold, rather than buy another sensor box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about a slow nursery season, not this mild AI tool. Five months is a cushion, but it is not a reason to stop watching the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the app get wrong last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sensor read wet because it sat under a dripping pipe, while the far beds were dry. My wife Ana’s paper chart showed the mismatch before the phone alert did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you install the app at her nursery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after she asks and we can test it without risking the plants. I will not use her business as an unpaid laboratory for my employer.

feel: **Uneasy** about nursery sales, with mild AI changes manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our team AI can write much of the alert code, so we should show customers what still needs a person’s check. I’d also tell junior developers to learn the tools rather than pretend the old ticket queue will return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own coding hours could shrink as software handles alerts and support questions. Ana’s nursery needs hands on plants for now, but her ordering and stock planning could move to AI too, so one cushion serves two risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI method for tracing false wet-soil alerts across sensor logs, using old cases and fake nursery names. In the first year I’d ask the manager which roles remain and look for paid greenhouse-tech openings if my developer hours fall, accepting only wages that cover our mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, but I would rather test a new method than argue that the old one will last. The risk is losing my pay while still paying for the children’s school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you test the false-alert method?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the dripping-pipe case and see whether the tool spots a wider problem. One wet sensor does not describe the whole greenhouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Ana to change her ordering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She knows her customers; I would not order plants for her because software predicts a sale. I could show her a report if she asks, and she would make the buying call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write my irrigation code and plan much of Ana’s nursery stock. Robots for hands-on planting and sensor installation may follow around 2031, so my desk work gets the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer wage could disappear while Ana still has plants to tend, but five months saved will not cover the mortgage forever. An installation job might buy time before robots spread, not a whole new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager now for a written date if software roles change, and Ana and I would keep the old delivery van instead of replacing it. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my developer job ends, I’d apply for paid greenhouse equipment installation only where vacancies exist and wages cover our bills; I would not buy a truck or tools on borrowed money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed but not still. A promised job is not the same as a paid order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say it still starts and gets the plants to customers, so a newer van can wait. We would keep money for the house and school before choosing a nicer vehicle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ana’s nursery hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is her business, and it cannot pay a second full wage just because I lose mine. I might help after school, but we would count the actual sales before calling that income.

I know **planting robots around 2031** come later than the software shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives growers and coders time to test which sensor problems really need a field visit. Robots may install equipment around 2034, so I would not tell anyone that ladder work is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn more about fitting sensors while I still have a salary, but AI could do much of the planning by 2031. Ana and I might build a bigger buffer if her sales and my wages hold, which matters before I take any risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take one paid Saturday sensor-installation job a month only if a grower books it, pays a parts deposit and Ana can cover childcare. I’d save the net fee after travel separately from 160 monthly we can save if both incomes hold; after 2031 I’d seek paid field-tech openings only if my developer role ends and vacancies cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but able to test whether the field work pays. A Saturday lost with the children has to leave more than a good photo of a sensor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might book the first Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A grower Ana knows has asked about a dry-bed alarm, but I would quote the job before agreeing. I already own basic tools; I would not buy a kit until a deposit pays for parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the first job falls through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my developer wage and let the side-income line stay at zero. I do not want my wife Ana to count a booking that never paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets families and growers choose tools by what works on a farm, not by a sales pitch. Robots for planting and installation may follow around 2039, after the code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but the mortgage may still need two incomes. I could build a year of expenses and see whether paid sensor work has repeat customers, though robots may later take much of the physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining irrigation code and take sensor jobs only when booked with a parts deposit and childcare covered. Separately, we’d save 180 monthly if both wages hold, aiming for a year of basic bills; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid equipment-service work only where vacancies remain and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about 2036, but the next few years look workable. I want a ledger of paid return calls before I tell my family this could replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a return call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A grower asks me back to fix a sensor I installed and actually pays the invoice. I would record travel, parts and the time I missed with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Ana to use AI more at the nursery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if she wants to test it against her own stock book. She owns the business and will decide what to buy, even if I write software for growers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my software wage could end while Ana’s nursery still needs the mortgage paid. A real paid installation opening that covers bills and a written job date would help, but robots around 2031 make field work a bridge rather than a guarantee.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who owns the nursery decisions. My wife Ana owns the nursery decisions, even if I write software for growers. I can show a tool, but she decides which plants to buy and which work pays.

headlineQuote: My wife Ana owns the nursery decisions, even if I write software for growers.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, ordinary pay and five months saved.
He and Ana support **two children** and a mortgage while her nursery sales vary by season.
He uses **AI daily** but checks sensor alerts against actual soil and Ana’s paper chart.
His **paid sensor jobs** require bookings, deposits and childcare, with net pay recorded.
The **2028 coding loss** worries him most; installation robots arrive later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his software pay while the household still relies on nursery sales.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date** and paid bill-covering installation opening would help, with later robots kept in view.
